claim: Eukaryotic replication origin licensing, activation and timing are influenced by chromatin.
source: Eukaryotic replication origin licensing, activation and timing are influenced by chromatin but a mechanistic understanding is lacking.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact that motivates the study.

claim: Nucleosomal organization influenced origin licensing during replication initiation.
source: Nucleosomal organization influenced two steps of replication initiation: origin licensing and helicase activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Nucleosomal organization influenced helicase activation during replication initiation.
source: Nucleosomal organization influenced two steps of replication initiation: origin licensing and helicase activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Local nucleosome positioning enhanced origin specificity.
source: Origin licensing assays showed that local nucleosome positioning enhanced origin specificity and modulated helicase loading by influencing ORC DNA binding.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1D.

claim: Local nucleosome positioning modulated helicase loading by influencing ORC DNA binding.
source: Origin licensing assays showed that local nucleosome positioning enhanced origin specificity and modulated helicase loading by influencing ORC DNA binding.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: SWI/SNF-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing.
source: Interestingly, SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing but showed reduced helicase activation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: RSC-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing.
source: Interestingly, SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing but showed reduced helicase activation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: SWI/SNF-remodeled nucleosomes showed reduced helicase activation.
source: Interestingly, SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing but showed reduced helicase activation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3D and 4.

claim: RSC-remodeled nucleosomes showed reduced helicase activation.
source: Interestingly, SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes were permissive for origin licensing but showed reduced helicase activation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 3D and 4.

claim: Specific CREs rescued replication of SWI/SNF and RSC templates if added prior to helicase activation.
source: Specific CREs rescued replication of these templates if added prior to helicase activation, indicating a permissive chromatin state must be established during origin licensing to allow efficient origin activation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: A permissive chromatin state must be established during origin licensing to allow efficient origin activation.
source: Specific CREs rescued replication of these templates if added prior to helicase activation, indicating a permissive chromatin state must be established during origin licensing to allow efficient origin activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Nucleosomes directly modulate origin licensing through distinct mechanisms.
source: Our studies show nucleosomes directly modulate origin licensing and activation through distinct mechanisms and provide insights into the regulation of replication initiation by chromatin.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Nucleosomes directly modulate origin activation through distinct mechanisms.
source: Our studies show nucleosomes directly modulate origin licensing and activation through distinct mechanisms and provide insights into the regulation of replication initiation by chromatin.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Each nucleosome consists of approximately 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.
source: Chromatin is primarily composed of nucleosomes, each of which consists of ~147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around a histone octamer.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about nucleosome structure.

claim: The location and modification state of nucleosomes is dynamic.
source: The location and modification state of nucleosomes is dynamic, regulates access to the DNA and partitions the genome into distinct chromatin states (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clapier and Cairns, 2009.

claim: Nucleosome positioning and modifications influence all DNA processes including replication, transcription, repair and recombination.
source: Nucleosome positioning and modifications influence all DNA processes including replication, transcription, repair and recombination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Maintaining appropriate chromatin states across the genome is critical for cellular viability.
source: Thus, maintaining appropriate chromatin states across the genome is critical for cellular viability (Hargreaves and Crabtree, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hargreaves and Crabtree, 2011.

claim: Proper eukaryotic DNA replication requires the temporal separation of origin licensing and origin activation.
source: Proper eukaryotic DNA replication requires the temporal separation of two key events: origin licensing and origin activation (Li and Araki, 2013; Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li and Araki, 2013 and Siddiqui et al., 2013.

claim: During G1, origin licensing is initiated by origin-recognition complex (ORC) binding to replication origin DNA.
source: During G1, origin licensing is initiated by origin-recognition complex (ORC) binding to replication origin DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the replication initiation process.

claim: ORC recruits Cdc6 and Cdt1 to load two inactive Mcm2-7 replicative DNA helicases around the origin DNA.
source: ORC then recruits Cdc6 and Cdt1 and these proteins load two inactive Mcm2-7 replicative DNA helicases around the origin DNA (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bell and Labib, 2016.

claim: Origin activation occurs during S phase.
source: Origin activation is temporally separated from origin licensing and occurs during S phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cell cycle timing of replication events.

claim: S-phase cyclin-dependent kinases and DDK drive recruitment of Cdc45 and GINS to form the active CMG complex.
source: S-phase cyclin-dependent kinases and the Dbf4-dependent Cdc7 kinase (DDK) drive recruitment of two helicase-activating proteins, Cdc45 and GINS, forming the active replicative helicase, the Cdc45/Mcm2-7/GINS (CMG) complex (Ilves et al., 2010; Tanaka and Araki, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ilves et al., 2010 and Tanaka and Araki, 2013.

claim: The majority of replication initiation events have been reconstituted in vitro using purified proteins and naked DNA.
source: The majority of these events have been reconstituted in vitro using purified proteins and naked DNA (Yeeles et al., 2015, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yeeles et al., 2015 and 2017.

claim: Origin DNA is nucleosome-free to allow ORC DNA binding.
source: Origin DNA is nucleosome-free to allow ORC DNA binding and, once bound, ORC positions origin-proximal nucleosomes (Berbenetz et al., 2010; Eaton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berbenetz et al., 2010 and Eaton et al., 2010.

claim: Once bound, ORC positions origin-proximal nucleosomes.
source: Origin DNA is nucleosome-free to allow ORC DNA binding and, once bound, ORC positions origin-proximal nucleosomes (Berbenetz et al., 2010; Eaton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berbenetz et al., 2010 and Eaton et al., 2010.

claim: Repositioning of origin-proximal nucleosomes reduces helicase loading and origin function.
source: Repositioning of origin-proximal nucleosomes reduces helicase loading and origin function (Lipford and Bell, 2001; Simpson, 1990), and loaded helicases appear to interact with these nucleosomes (Belsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lipford and Bell, 2001 and Simpson, 1990.

claim: Loaded helicases appear to interact with origin-proximal nucleosomes.
source: Repositioning of origin-proximal nucleosomes reduces helicase loading and origin function (Lipford and Bell, 2001; Simpson, 1990), and loaded helicases appear to interact with these nucleosomes (Belsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Belsky et al., 2015.

claim: Local chromatin states have been implicated in the activation of eukaryotic origins.
source: Local chromatin states have also been implicated in the activation of eukaryotic origins, each of which is predisposed to initiate earlier or later in S phase (Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rhind and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: CREs are multi-protein complexes that use the energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis to assemble, move, slide or alter the composition of nucleosomes.
source: CREs are multi-protein complexes that use the energy of ATP binding and hydrolysis to assemble, move, slide or alter the composition of nucleosomes (Clapier and Cairns, 2009; Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Clapier and Cairns, 2009 and Papamichos-Chronakis and Peterson, 2012.

claim: Four subfamilies of CREs are conserved from yeast to humans: ISWI, SWI/SNF, INO80, and CHD.
source: Four subfamilies of CREs are conserved from yeast to humans: ISWI, SWI/SNF, INO80, and CHD.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRE classification.

claim: Members of the ISWI subfamily typically function in nucleosome assembly and can create regularly spaced nucleosomal arrays by ATP-dependent sliding of nucleosomes.
source: Members of the ISWI and CHD subfamilies typically function in nucleosome assembly, and they can create regularly spaced nucleosomal arrays by ATP-dependent sliding of nucleosomes (Hamiche et al., 1999; Längst et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamiche et al., 1999 and Längst et al., 1999.

claim: Members of the CHD subfamily typically function in nucleosome assembly and can create regularly spaced nucleosomal arrays by ATP-dependent sliding of nucleosomes.
source: Members of the ISWI and CHD subfamilies typically function in nucleosome assembly, and they can create regularly spaced nucleosomal arrays by ATP-dependent sliding of nucleosomes (Hamiche et al., 1999; Längst et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hamiche et al., 1999 and Längst et al., 1999.

claim: Members of the SWI/SNF subfamily mobilize nucleosomes in cis and can evict nucleosomal histones or eject entire nucleosomes.
source: Similarly, members of the SWI/SNF subfamily mobilize nucleosomes in cis, but these enzymes can also evict nucleosomal histones or eject entire nucleosomes (Clapier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clapier et al., 2016.

claim: SWI/SNF subfamily CREs typically promote enhanced accessibility of nucleosomal DNA.
source: Consequently, these CREs typically promote enhanced accessibility of nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ability of SWI/SNF to evict histones and eject nucleosomes.

claim: Members of the INO80 subfamily conduct the post-replicative removal of a particular histone within a nucleosome and sequential replacement with either a canonical or a variant histone.
source: Finally, members of the INO80 subfamily conduct the post-replicative removal of a particular histone within a nucleosome, and sequential replacement with either a canonical or a variant histone, a process termed nucleosome editing (Mizuguchi et al., 2004; Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mizuguchi et al., 2004 and Papamichos-Chronakis et al., 2011.

claim: Some members of the INO80 subfamily can catalyze nucleosome sliding.
source: Notably, some members of the INO80 subfamily can also catalyze nucleosome sliding (e.g. yeast INO80-C) (Shen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shen et al., 2003.

claim: Different CREs use ATP-dependent DNA translocation as a central mechanism for their activities.
source: Although different CREs can exert a differential impact on nucleosomes, the current view is that each of these enzymes use ATP-dependent DNA translocation as a central mechanism for their activities.
evidence: This is stated as the current understanding in the field.

claim: ISW1-containing remodeling complexes interact with replisome proteins.
source: For instance, ISW1-containing remodeling complexes interact with replisome proteins (Poot et al., 2005) and Chd1 negatively regulate replication initiation (Biswas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Poot et al., 2005.

claim: Chd1 negatively regulates replication initiation.
source: For instance, ISW1-containing remodeling complexes interact with replisome proteins (Poot et al., 2005) and Chd1 negatively regulate replication initiation (Biswas et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Biswas et al., 2008.

claim: SWI/SNF stimulates replication initiation at specific yeast origins.
source: Similarly, SWI/SNF stimulates replication initiation at specific yeast origins (Flanagan and Peterson, 1999) and is associated with a subset of human origins (Euskirchen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Flanagan and Peterson, 1999.

claim: SWI/SNF is associated with a subset of human origins.
source: Similarly, SWI/SNF stimulates replication initiation at specific yeast origins (Flanagan and Peterson, 1999) and is associated with a subset of human origins (Euskirchen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Euskirchen et al., 2011.

claim: ISW1a-remodeled nucleosomal DNA templates showed levels of Mcm2-7 loading comparable to naked DNA templates.
source: The amount of ORC DNA binding, helicase association (low-salt wash [L]) and helicase loading (high-salt wash [H]) were comparable between nucleosomal and naked DNA templates (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ISW1a-remodeled nucleosomes are permissive for origin licensing.
source: Thus, ISW1a-remodeled nucleosomes are permissive for origin licensing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 1C showing comparable helicase loading on ISW1a templates and naked DNA.

claim: Nucleosome assembly reduced non-specific Mcm2-7 loading onto mutant ARS1-containing DNA without altering helicase loading onto WT DNA.
source: Under these conditions, nucleosome assembly reduced non-specific Mcm2-7 loading onto mutant ARS1-containing DNA without altering helicase loading onto WT DNA (Figure 1D, top panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Nucleosomes reduced origin licensing at non-origin DNA sequences.
source: Thus, nucleosomes reduced origin licensing at non-origin DNA sequences, consistent with previous in vivo studies implicating local nucleosomes in origin selection (Berbenetz et al., 2010; Eaton et al., 2010).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 1D and is consistent with cited in vivo studies.

claim: ISW1a, ISW1b, INO80-C, ISW2 and Chd1 each resulted in regularly-spaced nucleosomes on the origin DNA.
source: ISW1a, ISW1b, INO80-C, ISW2 and Chd1 each resulted in regularly-spaced nucleosomes on the origin DNA, albeit with different spacings (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase digestion patterns shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes did not show evidence of uniformly-spaced nucleosomes.
source: In contrast, SWI/SNF- and RSC-remodeled nucleosomes did not show evidence of uniformly-spaced nucleosomes, consistent with previous observations (Flaus and Owen-Hughes, 2003; Kassabov et al., 2003).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase digestion patterns shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with cited previous observations.

claim: The presence of different CREs did not dramatically change the extent of nucleosome formation.
source: These studies showed that the presence of different CREs did not dramatically change the extent of nucleosome formation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: ISW1b and INO80-C templates showed modest reductions in loaded Mcm2-7.
source: ISW1b and INO80-C templates showed modest reductions in loaded Mcm2-7 and Chd1 and ISW2 templates showed progressively less loading.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Chd1 and ISW2 templates showed progressively less Mcm2-7 loading.
source: ISW1b and INO80-C templates showed modest reductions in loaded Mcm2-7 and Chd1 and ISW2 templates showed progressively less loading.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The CRE present during nucleosomal assembly impacted the extent of origin licensing.
source: Thus, the CRE present during nucleosomal assembly impacted the extent of origin licensing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential helicase loading observed for different CRE-remodeled templates shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The ISW1a template showed a nucleosome-free region (NFR) overlapping ARS1 with well-defined flanking nucleosomes.
source: The ISW1a template showed a nucleosome-free region (NFR) overlapping ARS1 with well-defined flanking nucleosomes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ISW2 template showed the appearance of a positioned nucleosome overlapping the origin centered at −54 bp relative to ACS.
source: In contrast, ISW2 template showed the appearance of a positioned nucleosome overlapping the origin (centered at −54 bp relative to ACS, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The flanking nucleosome on the opposite side of the origin was shifted towards the ACS (from +222 to +168) in the ISW2 templates.
source: In addition, the flanking nucleosome on the opposite side of the origin was shifted towards the ACS (from +222 to +168) in the ISW2 templates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Encroachment of origin-proximal nucleosomes onto origin DNA directly inhibits origin licensing.
source: These data support a model in which encroachment of origin-proximal nucleosomes onto origin DNA directly inhibits origin licensing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing reduced helicase loading on ISW2 templates that have nucleosomes positioned over the origin.

claim: The extent of ORC binding to the ISW2 and Chd1 templates correlated with the amount of Mcm2-7 loading.
source: The extent of ORC binding to the ISW2 and Chd1 templates correlated with the amount of Mcm2-7 loading (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the data in Figure 2B and Figure 2D.

claim: When ORC bound DNA prior to Chd1- or ISW2-directed nucleosome assembly, loaded Mcm2-7 levels were restored to levels similar to ISW1a templates.
source: Importantly, when ORC bound DNA prior to Chd1- or ISW2-directed nucleosome assembly, loaded Mcm2-7 levels were restored to levels similar to ISW1a templates (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Nucleosome positioning over the origin reduces origin licensing by inhibiting ORC DNA binding.
source: Together, these data indicate that nucleosome positioning over the origin reduces origin licensing by inhibiting ORC DNA binding and that ORC is not sufficient to move nucleosomes in the absence of a CRE.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figures 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: ORC is not sufficient to move nucleosomes in the absence of a CRE.
source: Together, these data indicate that nucleosome positioning over the origin reduces origin licensing by inhibiting ORC DNA binding and that ORC is not sufficient to move nucleosomes in the absence of a CRE.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 2E showing that ORC must be present before nucleosome assembly to prevent inhibition.

claim: ORC and ORC∆BAH showed comparable levels of helicase loading onto all the nucleosomal templates.
source: Consistent with the limited effect of deletion of the Orc1 BAH domain on ARS1 function in vivo (Müller et al., 2010), ORC and ORC∆BAH showed comparable levels of helicase loading onto all the nucleosomal templates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C and is consistent with cited in vivo studies.

claim: Addition of purified Abf1 to either naked DNA or ISW1a templates did not improve helicase loading.
source: Addition of purified Abf1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) to either naked DNA or ISW1a templates did not improve helicase loading (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Abf1 did not improve helicase loading on the ISW2 template.
source: In contrast to ORC, Abf1 did not improve helicase loading on the ISW2 template (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: ISW1a templates showed comparable levels of replication products to that of naked DNA.
source: ISW1a templates showed comparable levels of replication products to that of naked DNA (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nucleotide incorporation was Cdc6-dependent.
source: Nucleotide incorporation was Cdc6- (Figure 3B), DDK- (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—source data 1) and origin-sequence-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that the DNA synthesis observed was due to replication initiation and elongation (rather than DNA repair).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nucleotide incorporation was DDK-dependent.
source: Nucleotide incorporation was Cdc6- (Figure 3B), DDK- (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—source data 1) and origin-sequence-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that the DNA synthesis observed was due to replication initiation and elongation (rather than DNA repair).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Nucleotide incorporation was origin-sequence-dependent.
source: Nucleotide incorporation was Cdc6- (Figure 3B), DDK- (Figure 3C, and Figure 3—source data 1) and origin-sequence-dependent (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that the DNA synthesis observed was due to replication initiation and elongation (rather than DNA repair).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: For ISW1a, ISW1b, ISW2, INO80-C and Chd1 templates, the level of replication products closely matched the amount of helicase loading with the same templates.
source: For ISW1a, ISW1b, ISW2, INO80-C and Chd1, the level of replication products closely matched the amount of helicase loading with the same templates (compare Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the data in Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Origin activation and replisome assembly were not further reduced by ISW1a, ISW1b, ISW2, INO80-C and Chd1 nucleosomal templates.
source: Thus, origin activation and replisome assembly were not further reduced by these nucleosomal templates.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that replication levels matched helicase loading levels for these templates.

claim: SWI/SNF, RSC and ISW1a templates showed comparable levels of Mcm2-7 loading.
source: SWI/SNF, RSC and ISW1a templates showed comparable levels of Mcm2-7 loading (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), but the amount of replication products from SWI/SNF and RSC templates was reduced ~5 fold relative to ISW1a templates (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The amount of replication products from SWI/SNF and RSC templates was reduced approximately 5 fold relative to ISW1a templates.
source: SWI/SNF, RSC and ISW1a templates showed comparable levels of Mcm2-7 loading (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), but the amount of replication products from SWI/SNF and RSC templates was reduced ~5 fold relative to ISW1a templates (Figure 3D and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Nucleosomal DNA templates remodeled by SWI/SNF and RSC inhibit one or more events downstream of origin licensing.
source: Thus, nucleosomal DNA templates remodeled by SWI/SNF and RSC inhibit one or more events downstream of origin licensing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that SWI/SNF and RSC templates show normal helicase loading but reduced replication.

claim: ISW1a templates showed reduced replication using the fully-reconstituted assay compared to the S-phase-extract-based assay.
source: Compared to the S-phase-extract-based assay, ISW1a templates showed reduced replication using the fully-reconstituted assay (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), most likely due to a lack of CREs and histone chaperones present in the S-phase-extract-based assay (Devbhandari et al., 2017; Kurat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and is explained by cited references.

claim: Replication of the SWI/SNF and RSC templates was similarly reduced relative to their ISW1a-remodeled counterpart using the reconstituted assay.
source: Nevertheless, replication of the SWI/SNF and RSC templates was similarly reduced relative to their ISW1a-remodeled counterpart using the reconstituted assay (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The reduced replication capacity of the RSC and SWI/SNF templates requires the activity of the corresponding CRE.
source: Thus, the reduced replication capacity of the RSC and SWI/SNF templates requires the activity of the corresponding CRE.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B showing that nucleosomes assembled without a CRE do not show reduced replication.

claim: DDK phosphorylation of Mcm2-7 was either unchanged (SWI/SNF) or improved (RSC) relative to ISW1a templates.
source: This modification was either unchanged (SWI/SNF) or improved (RSC) relative to ISW1a templates (Figure 4C), indicating Mcm2-7 phosphorylation by DDK was not reduced.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mcm2-7 phosphorylation by DDK was not reduced on SWI/SNF and RSC templates.
source: This modification was either unchanged (SWI/SNF) or improved (RSC) relative to ISW1a templates (Figure 4C), indicating Mcm2-7 phosphorylation by DDK was not reduced.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Both SWI/SNF and RSC templates showed reduced Cdc45 and GINS template association compared to ISW1a templates.
source: Both SWI/SNF and RSC templates showed reduced Cdc45 and GINS template association compared to ISW1a templates.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The observed reduction in DNA replication products observed for the SWI/SNF and RSC templates was due to reduced CMG formation and helicase activation.
source: Thus, the observed reduction in DNA replication products observed for the SWI/SNF and RSC templates in the complete assays was due to reduced CMG formation and helicase activation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 4E showing reduced Cdc45, GINS, and Rfa1 association under conditions that allow CMG formation but not elongation.

claim: Adding ISW1a during the helicase-loading step restored CMG formation and increased DNA replication of the RSC templates.
source: Adding ISW1a during the helicase-loading step (DL) of the assay (Figure 5A) restored CMG formation and increased DNA replication of the RSC templates (Figure 5B, compare lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Adding RSC during the helicase-loading step did not alter either the amount of replication or CMG formation on RSC templates.
source: In contrast, adding RSC during the helicase-loading step did not alter either the amount of replication or CMG formation (Figure 5B, lane 6).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Addition of ISW1a improved replication of SWI/SNF templates.
source: Similar experiments with SWI/SNF templates showed that the addition of ISW1a (but not SWI/SNF) improved replication of SWI/SNF templates (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of RSC or SWI/SNF to ISW1a templates during helicase loading did not reduce replication levels.
source: In contrast to the ability of ISW1a to improve replication from the RSC and SWI/SNF templates, addition of RSC or SWI/SNF to ISW1a templates during helicase loading did not reduce replication levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of Chd1 to ISW1a during helicase loading reduced replication.
source: Interestingly, consistent with its ability to reduce helicase loading, addition of Chd1 to ISW1a during helicase loading did reduce replication.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Specific CREs create nucleosomal states that facilitate CMG formation and replication initiation.
source: Instead, our findings suggest that specific CREs create nucleosomal states that facilitate CMG formation and replication initiation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing that ISW1a can rescue RSC and SWI/SNF templates but RSC and SWI/SNF cannot.

claim: There was no apparent correlation between flanking nucleosome positions and the reduced origin activation observed for SWI/SNF and RSC templates.
source: Thus, unlike the situation for origin licensing (Figure 2), there was no apparent correlation between flanking nucleosome positions and the reduced origin activation observed for SWI/SNF and RSC templates.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Incorporation of the Mcm2 histone-binding motif mutation did not alter helicase loading or DNA synthesis with or without nucleosomes.
source: Incorporation of this mutation did not alter helicase loading or DNA synthesis with or without nucleosomes (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B), suggesting that this interaction is not critical for replication initiation under the conditions of these assays.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A–B.

claim: Addition of ISW1b or INO80-C to RSC templates after helicase loading improved replication initiation and CMG formation to similar levels as ISW1a addition.
source: In contrast, addition of ISW1b or INO80-C to RSC templates after helicase loading improved replication initiation and CMG formation to similar levels as ISW1a addition (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The ability to restore full replication competence to the RSC or SWI/SNF templates is limited to a subset of CREs.
source: Thus, the ability to restore full replication competence to the RSC or SWI/SNF templates is limited to a subset of CREs, consistent with previous studies indicating that these complexes have distinct functionalities (Clapier and Cairns, 2009).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 5C and is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: When ISW1a was added only during the helicase-loading step or after helicase-loading but removed before DDK treatment, ISW1a significantly improved replication of the SWI/SNF and RSC templates.
source: When added only during the helicase-loading step (DL) or after helicase-loading but removed before DDK treatment (AL), ISW1a significantly improved replication of the SWI/SNF (Figure 5D) and RSC templates (Figure 5B and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 5B, 5D, and 5E.

claim: Addition of ISW1a only during the initiation/elongation step of the replication reaction did not improve CMG formation or replication of RSC or SWI/SNF templates.
source: In contrast, addition of ISW1a only during the initiation/elongation (I/E) step of the replication reaction did not improve CMG formation or replication of RSC (Figure 5B) or SWI/SNF templates (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 5B and 5D.

claim: ISW1a can only improve the replication competence of RSC and SWI/SNF templates if it acts prior to the events of origin activation.
source: Thus, ISW1a can only improve the replication competence of RSC and SWI/SNF templates if it acts prior to the events of origin activation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data showing that ISW1a addition during or after helicase loading improves replication, but addition during initiation/elongation does not.

claim: Local nucleosomes directly impact two steps in replication initiation: ORC DNA binding and CMG formation.
source: Together these studies reveal that local nucleosomes directly impact two steps in replication initiation: ORC DNA binding and CMG formation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion stated in the Discussion and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Only a subset of CREs positioned nucleosomes in a manner that allowed efficient origin licensing.
source: Only a subset of CREs positioned nucleosomes in a manner that allowed efficient origin licensing (Figures 2B, 6A and B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ISW2 templates showed the most inefficient Mcm2-7 loading compared to other templates.
source: ISW2 templates showed the most inefficient Mcm2-7 loading compared to other templates and this reduction correlated with the encroachment of origin-proximal nucleosomes over origin DNA in a manner that inhibited ORC DNA binding (Figures 2C and 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: The reduction in Mcm2-7 loading on ISW2 templates correlated with the encroachment of origin-proximal nucleosomes over origin DNA in a manner that inhibited ORC DNA binding.
source: ISW2 templates showed the most inefficient Mcm2-7 loading compared to other templates and this reduction correlated with the encroachment of origin-proximal nucleosomes over origin DNA in a manner that inhibited ORC DNA binding (Figures 2C and 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: ISW2 slides nucleosomes towards the promoter-proximal NFR to suppress transcription at cryptic transcription-start sites.
source: This finding is consistent with studies showing that ISW2 slides nucleosomes towards the promoter-proximal NFR to suppress transcription at cryptic transcription-start sites (Whitehouse et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Whitehouse et al., 2007.

claim: Once ORC is bound to origin DNA, ISW2 is unable to displace ORC with a nucleosome.
source: Interestingly, once ORC is bound to origin DNA, ISW2 is unable to displace ORC with a nucleosome (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Once ISW2 establishes nucleosome positioning at the origin, ORC is unable to bind.
source: Similarly, once ISW2 establishes nucleosome positioning at the origin, ORC is unable to bind (Figure 2E), suggesting ORC cannot displace interfering nucleosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ORC cannot displace interfering nucleosomes.
source: Similarly, once ISW2 establishes nucleosome positioning at the origin, ORC is unable to bind (Figure 2E), suggesting ORC cannot displace interfering nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both the relative timing of ORC binding and histone deposition and the CRE present at this time will influence the use of a given site as an origin.
source: These findings suggest that both the relative timing of ORC binding and histone deposition and the CRE present at this time will influence the use of a given site as an origin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing that ORC and ISW2 cannot displace each other once established.

claim: The lack of a role for the ORC BAH domain is expected given the modest effect of deletion of the BAH domain on ARS1 replication initiation in vivo.
source: The lack of a role for the ORC BAH domain is expected given the modest effect of deletion of the BAH domain on ARS1 replication initiation in vivo (Müller et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Müller et al., 2010.

claim: It is possible that the Orc1 BAH domain was not observed to have a role due to the unmodified status of the histones used in these experiments.
source: Given the observation that other BAH domains recognize specific modified forms of nucleosomes (Yang and Xu, 2013), it is also possible that we did not observe a role for the Orc1 BAH domain due to the unmodified status of the histones used in these experiments.
evidence: This is speculation based on cited knowledge about BAH domain function.

claim: Abf1 binding positions nucleosomes on one side of ARS1 in vivo, however, ORC is able to perform this function in the absence of Abf1 at many origins.
source: Abf1 binding positions nucleosomes on one side of ARS1 in vivo, however, ORC is able to perform this function in the absence of Abf1 at many origins (Eaton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eaton et al., 2010.

claim: It is possible that Abf1 binding is important to position nucleosomes in the presence of invasive transcription but not in the absence.
source: Thus, it is possible that Abf1 binding is important to position nucleosomes in the presence of this invasive transcription but not in the absence (such as in our experiments).
evidence: This is speculation to explain why Abf1 did not have an effect in the in vitro experiments.

claim: The reduced replication of RSC and SWI/SNF templates is rescued by addition of other CREs.
source: Our finding that the reduced replication of these templates is rescued by addition of other CREs (Figure 5) makes it clear that these effects are nucleosome-dependent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The effects of RSC and SWI/SNF templates on replication are nucleosome-dependent.
source: Our finding that the reduced replication of these templates is rescued by addition of other CREs (Figure 5) makes it clear that these effects are nucleosome-dependent.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Simple steric inhibition by encroaching nucleosomes is unlikely to explain the reduced CMG formation on RSC and SWI/SNF templates.
source: Given that these templates allow efficient helicase loading, simple steric inhibition by encroaching nucleosomes is unlikely to explain these effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that helicase loading is normal on these templates.

claim: ISW1a and SWI/SNF templates had a similar pattern of surrounding nucleosomes.
source: Indeed, despite their different capacities for replication initiation and CMG formation, ISW1a and SWI/SNF templates had a similar pattern of surrounding nucleosomes and the SWI/SNF nucleosomes pattern was not changed by the same ISW1a addition that restored robust CMG formation and replication initiation to these templates (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SWI/SNF nucleosomes pattern was not changed by ISW1a addition that restored robust CMG formation and replication initiation to these templates.
source: Indeed, despite their different capacities for replication initiation and CMG formation, ISW1a and SWI/SNF templates had a similar pattern of surrounding nucleosomes and the SWI/SNF nucleosomes pattern was not changed by the same ISW1a addition that restored robust CMG formation and replication initiation to these templates (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MNase-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that SWI/SNF family remodelers establish nucleosome structures that are different from canonical nucleosomes.
source: Previous studies have suggested that SWI/SNF family remodelers establish nucleosome structures that are different from canonical nucleosomes (Lorch et al., 1998; Schnitzler et al., 1998; Ulyanova and Schnitzler, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lorch et al., 1998, Schnitzler et al., 1998, and Ulyanova and Schnitzler, 2005.

claim: SWI/SNF and RSC are known to remove H2A/H2B dimers from nucleosomes.
source: SWI/SNF and RSC are also known to remove H2A/H2B dimers from nucleosomes (Clapier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clapier et al., 2016.

claim: Recent studies suggest that loaded Mcm2-7 interacts with adjacent nucleosomes.
source: One interesting possibility to explain the different capacities of the templates to facilitate CMG formation is raised by recent studies suggesting that loaded Mcm2-7 interacts with adjacent nucleosomes (Belsky et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Belsky et al., 2015.

claim: Different positions/conformations of local nucleosomes may impact the ability of nucleosomes to interact with Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
source: It is possible that different positions/conformations of local nucleosomes (see below) impacts the ability of nucleosomes to interact with Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the differential effects of different CRE-remodeled templates.

claim: Interactions between nucleosomes and Mcm2-7 could directly or indirectly modulate access of helicase-activating proteins to loaded Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
source: These interactions could directly or indirectly modulate access of helicase-activating proteins to loaded Mcm2-7 double hexamers.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism by which nucleosomes affect CMG formation.

claim: A positive interaction between loaded Mcm2-7 and nucleosomes must be established prior to CMG formation.
source: Addition of some CREs to RSC or SWI/SNF templates improved their replication but only if added before the helicase-activation proteins (Figure 5), suggesting that a positive interaction between loaded Mcm2-7 and nucleosomes must be established prior to CMG formation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A subset of CREs produce nucleosomes that can interact with the replication machinery positively and once these interactions are established they prevent other CREs from inducing alternative conformations.
source: Perhaps a subset of CREs produce nucleosomes that can interact with the replication machinery positively and once these interactions are established they prevent other CREs from inducing alternative conformations.
evidence: This is speculation to explain why RSC and SWI/SNF cannot reduce replication from ISW1a templates when added during helicase loading.

claim: The different CREs are not equivalent in their ability to establish replication-competent nucleosomes.
source: Our studies show that the different CREs are not equivalent in their ability to establish replication-competent nucleosomes.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data throughout the manuscript showing differential effects of different CREs.

claim: The specificity of the different CREs suggests that the presence of different CREs at origins will impact origin usage.
source: The specificity of the different CREs in our assays suggests that the presence of different CREs at origins will impact origin usage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of different CREs observed in the experiments.

claim: A CRE present during S phase would impact the initial assembly of nucleosomes and more likely impact subsequent origin licensing/helicase loading.
source: A CRE present during S phase would impact the initial assembly of nucleosomes and more likely impact subsequent origin licensing/helicase loading.
evidence: This is an inference about the in vivo implications of the findings.

claim: A CRE that is present during G1 is less likely to impact origin licensing and more likely to modulate subsequent CMG formation.
source: A CRE that is present during G1 is less likely to impact origin licensing and more likely to modulate subsequent CMG formation.
evidence: This is an inference about the in vivo implications of the findings.

claim: The RSC and SWI/SNF templates show hallmarks of late-initiating origins.
source: Interestingly, the RSC and SWI/SNF templates show hallmarks of late-initiating origins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data comparing the properties of these templates to known properties of late origins.

claim: Like late-initiating origins, RSC and SWI/SNF templates showed efficient origin licensing but reduced/delayed replication initiation.
source: Like late-initiating origins (Belsky et al., 2015; Santocanale et al., 1999; Wyrick et al., 2001), these templates showed efficient origin licensing but reduced/delayed replication initiation.
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to Belsky et al., 2015, Santocanale et al., 1999, and Wyrick et al., 2001.

claim: Replication timing is established in late M or early G1 phase.
source: In addition, replication timing is established in late M or early G1 phase (Dimitrova and Gilbert, 1999; Raghuraman et al., 1997) and replication timing can only be reprogrammed prior to S phase (Peace et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dimitrova and Gilbert, 1999 and Raghuraman et al., 1997.

claim: Replication timing can only be reprogrammed prior to S phase.
source: In addition, replication timing is established in late M or early G1 phase (Dimitrova and Gilbert, 1999; Raghuraman et al., 1997) and replication timing can only be reprogrammed prior to S phase (Peace et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Peace et al., 2016.

claim: SWI/SNF and RSC templates can be remodeled to replicate efficiently if certain CREs are added prior to shifting the templates into helicase-activation conditions.
source: Similarly, SWI/SNF and RSC templates can be remodeled to replicate efficiently if certain CREs are added prior to shifting the templates into helicase-activation conditions (Figure 5B), which is the biochemical equivalent of the G1-S phase transition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Local nucleosome states influence replication timing.
source: These similarities suggest that local nucleosome states influence replication timing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarities between the properties of RSC/SWI/SNF templates and late-initiating origins.

claim: Origin-proximal nucleosome-free regions are a common characteristic of origins in many organisms.
source: Although most organisms do not use sequence-defined origins of replication, origin-proximal nucleosome-free regions are a common characteristic of origins in many organisms (Fragkos et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fragkos et al., 2015.

claim: The findings regarding the impact of local nucleosomes on origin licensing and selection are relevant to origins in organisms that do not use sequence-defined origins.
source: Thus, our findings regarding the impact of local nucleosomes on origin licensing and selection are relevant to these origins as well.
evidence: This is an inference about the broader applicability of the findings.

claim: Once helicases are loaded, specific origin sequences have little or no impact on subsequent origin activation.
source: Importantly, once helicases are loaded, specific origin sequences have little or no impact on subsequent origin activation (Gros et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gros et al., 2014 and 2015.
